topics.title: Start here
topics.heading: System design topics: start here
topics.one_line: Start with common system design principles and their pros and cons.

summary.what: A starting set of learning resources for common system design principles.
summary.job: It helps new learners review scalability topics before trade-offs and building blocks.
summary.tradeoff: Everything is a trade-off.

topics.title: Study guide
topics.heading: Study guide
topics.one_line: Plan system design study for a short, medium, or long interview timeline.

summary.what: A suggested set of topics to review for an interview timeline.
summary.job: It helps you choose breadth, depth, and practice based on your timeline.
summary.tradeoff: Interview questions depend on experience, background, role, company, and luck.

topics.title: Interview approach
topics.heading: How to approach a system design interview question
topics.one_line: Lead an open-ended design interview with a clear sequence of steps.

summary.what: A guide for tackling a system design interview question.
summary.job: It guides you through requirements, a high-level design, core parts, and scale.
summary.tradeoff: Discuss potential solutions and trade-offs when you address bottlenecks.

topics.title: Performance vs scalability
topics.heading: Performance vs scalability
topics.one_line: Separate a slow system for one user from one that slows under load.

summary.what: A service is scalable when added resources increase performance in proportion.
summary.job: It helps distinguish a single-user performance problem from a heavy-load scalability problem.
summary.tradeoff: More performance can mean serving more work or handling larger work units.

topics.title: Latency vs throughput
topics.heading: Latency vs throughput
topics.one_line: Balance time for one action against actions completed over time.

summary.what: Latency is the time for an action or result. Throughput is actions or results per unit of time.
summary.job: It helps set a goal of high throughput with acceptable latency.
summary.tradeoff: Aim for maximal throughput with acceptable latency.

topics.title: Availability vs consistency
topics.heading: Availability vs consistency
topics.one_line: Choose how a distributed system handles current data and continued responses.

summary.what: CAP describes consistency, availability, and tolerance of network partitions.
summary.job: It helps choose guarantees for a distributed computer system during network failures.
summary.tradeoff: Networks are not reliable, so partition tolerance requires a choice between consistency and availability.

topics.title: Consistency patterns
topics.heading: Consistency patterns
topics.one_line: Choose how copies of data synchronize for client reads.

summary.what: Weak, eventual, and strong consistency describe when reads see a write.
summary.job: It helps synchronize multiple data copies so clients have a consistent view.
summary.tradeoff: Weak reads might not see a write; strong consistency replicates data synchronously.

topics.title: Availability patterns
topics.heading: Availability patterns
topics.one_line: Use fail-over and replication to support high availability.

summary.what: Fail-over and replication are complementary patterns for high availability.
summary.job: They keep a service available when a server or component fails.
summary.tradeoff: Fail-over adds hardware and complexity, and failure before replication can lose data.

topics.title: Domain name system
topics.heading: Domain name system
topics.one_line: Translate a domain name to an IP address.

summary.what: DNS translates a domain name to an IP address.
summary.job: It tells clients which server to contact during a lookup.
summary.tradeoff: DNS access adds a slight delay, and cached mappings can become stale.

topics.title: Content delivery network
topics.heading: Content delivery network
topics.one_line: Serve content from proxy servers close to users.

summary.what: A CDN is a global network of proxy servers that serves content near users.
summary.job: It serves static files and keeps fulfilled requests off your servers.
summary.tradeoff: Costs can be significant, and content can be stale before its TTL expires.

topics.title: Load balancer
topics.heading: Load balancer
topics.one_line: Distribute client requests across computing resources.

summary.what: A load balancer distributes incoming client requests to computing resources.
summary.job: It avoids unhealthy or overloaded servers and can reduce a single point of failure.
summary.tradeoff: It can become a bottleneck, and multiple load balancers add complexity.

topics.title: Reverse proxy
topics.heading: Reverse proxy (web server)
topics.one_line: Give public clients one interface to internal services.

summary.what: A reverse proxy is a web server that centralizes internal services for the public.
summary.job: It forwards a client request to a server and returns that server's response.
summary.tradeoff: A single reverse proxy is a single point of failure; more proxies add complexity.

topics.title: Application layer
topics.heading: Application layer
topics.one_line: Separate application services from the web layer.

summary.what: The application layer can be separated from the web layer.
summary.job: It lets each layer scale and be configured independently.
summary.tradeoff: Loosely coupled services and microservices add deployment and operations complexity.

topics.title: Database
topics.heading: Database
topics.one_line: Store data and use patterns that help it scale.

summary.what: This section covers relational databases and NoSQL databases.
summary.job: It describes ways to scale a relational database, including replication, federation, and sharding.
summary.tradeoff: Replication, federation, and sharding add hardware and complexity.

topics.title: Cache
topics.heading: Cache
topics.one_line: Reuse prior results to speed page loads and reduce system load.

summary.what: A cache stores prior results so a request can avoid the original work.
summary.job: It improves page load times and reduces load on servers and databases.
summary.tradeoff: Cache invalidation is difficult, and caches must stay consistent with the source of truth.

topics.title: Asynchronism
topics.heading: Asynchronism
topics.one_line: Move expensive work out of the request path.

summary.what: Asynchronous workflows run expensive work outside the request path.
summary.job: They reduce request times and can prepare time-consuming work in advance.
summary.tradeoff: Queues add delays and complexity, so inexpensive or real-time work can suit synchronous operations.

topics.title: Communication
topics.heading: Communication
topics.one_line: Compare ways clients and servers exchange data.

summary.what: This section covers HTTP, TCP, UDP, RPC, and REST.
summary.job: It helps choose how clients and servers exchange requests, responses, and data.
summary.tradeoff: TCP guarantees add delay; UDP is more efficient but less reliable.

topics.title: Security
topics.heading: Security
topics.one_line: Cover basic steps that protect system data and inputs.

summary.what: Security is a broad topic. The primer covers basic security steps.
summary.job: It helps protect data, sanitize inputs, prevent SQL injection, and limit access.
summary.tradeoff: Unless a role requires it, the primer says basic security knowledge may be enough.

topics.title: Powers of two table
topics.heading: Powers of two table
topics.one_line: A table of powers of two and common byte sizes.

summary.what: A table lists powers of two with common counts and byte sizes.
summary.job: It is useful for back-of-the-envelope calculations.
summary.tradeoff: None stated in the primer.

topics.title: Latency numbers
topics.heading: Latency numbers every programmer should know
topics.one_line: Compare latency and throughput figures for common computer operations.

summary.what: A table compares latency for common computer and network operations.
summary.job: It provides handy metrics for back-of-the-envelope calculations.
summary.tradeoff: None stated in the primer.

topics.title: Additional interview questions
topics.heading: Additional system design interview questions
topics.one_line: Common design interview questions with links to solution resources.

summary.what: A list of common system design interview questions with resource links.
summary.job: It helps you find resources on how to solve each question.
summary.tradeoff: None stated in the primer.

topics.title: Real world architectures
topics.heading: Real world architectures
topics.one_line: Articles about how real systems are designed.

summary.what: A collection of articles on how real world systems are designed.
summary.job: It helps identify shared principles, technologies, patterns, and lessons learned.
summary.tradeoff: Do not focus on the small details in these articles.

topics.title: Company architectures
topics.heading: Company architectures
topics.one_line: Architecture references for a range of companies.

summary.what: A list of companies with links to architecture references.
summary.job: It helps you find architecture material for named companies.
summary.tradeoff: None stated in the primer.

topics.title: Company engineering blogs
topics.heading: Company engineering blogs
topics.one_line: Engineering blogs for companies where you may interview.

summary.what: A list of engineering blogs from many companies.
summary.job: It helps you study architectures from companies where you are interviewing.
summary.tradeoff: Questions you encounter might come from the same domain.
